title: Please Don’t Squeeze the Tomatoes! | The Tyee
text:
People in B.C. are headed to the polls in October for municipal elections across the province.

At the same time, local newsrooms have been gutted, with existing reporting teams trying to do more with less.

Local politics are hugely consequential for how we live day to day but often have the lowest voter turnouts of any kinds of elections.

The Tyee’s independent journalists are on the ground, tracking candidates and issues across the province.

And we’re asking our readers what is most important to you this civic election season.

That’s because we work for you. Our non-profit newsroom is funded in large part directly by our readers, who we call Tyee Builders. As a Builder, you can contribute an amount that works for you, on your schedule, and help support the public interest journalism that is crucial during the democratic process. And because we’re a registered journalism organization, you’ll get a tax receipt for your contribution over $5.

Every dollar received from our readers ensures our talented team of journalists can get to work and make our reporting available to the public, free of charge, no paywall.

Support good journalism during election season and become a Tyee Builder today.

— Jeanette Ageson, Publisher

You made it all the way to the bottom of the article. That makes you some serious Tyee Builder material.

What’s a Tyee Builder, you ask? It’s a person, a reader, who has decided they want to be part of the team that helps keep open-access, public interest journalism alive.

Without them, without you, the Tyee’s newsroom, staffed with fiercely independent reporters and editors, would not be able to devote all their time to getting to the truth and sharing it freely with the world.

The Tyee is not part of a big news chain or owned by people who are trying to turn a profit. Our non-profit newsroom doesn’t stuff our pages with annoying ads or lock our work behind a paywall. But we still have bills to pay, and good journalism costs a lot. The only way we can square this circle is if a certain percentage of our readers agree to support our newsroom. And luckily, over 10,000 people have decided to do so.

With the help of our readers, we’ve bucked the doom and gloom trend in Canadian media – we’ve grown our team, reach more people than ever, and publish impactful journalism that sparks conversations, reveals truths and moves social change.

Back the team that powers our newsroom – you choose the amount, the frequency, and you can cancel at any time. Plus, you’ll get a tax receipt for your contributions over $5.

If you value the work The Tyee does, please consider becoming a Tyee Builder today.

— Jeanette Ageson, Publisher

Have you ever wandered through a market in peak tomato season? That sunshine smell hitting your nostrils, drawing your attention to the inglorious folded and bulbous fruits carefully arranged in trays and rows of boxes overflowing with bite-sized red, purple and yellow snacks. Have you ever caught a farmer’s eye when you couldn’t resist squeezing one? Behind that tomato on your dinner table is a complex infrastructural dynamic: a farm, workers, a truck, a market stall, a permit, a public space, a neighbourhood — all part of a direct system that gets food from a field outside of the city into the hands of the people who live and work here. And increasingly, the system itself is being squeezed!

Vancouver Farmers Markets has been operating farmers markets in the city of Vancouver for more than 30 years. Today, our nine neighbourhood markets welcome thousands of visitors each year (675,000 in 2025) and create direct selling opportunities for hundreds of local farms and small businesses. In 2025, there were 264 vendors; 66 were new entrants, 147 were women-owned, 51 were youth-run, and 115 were BIPOC businesses.

The increased visits, long vendor wait-list and record sales clearly indicate that farmers markets are in high demand. And yet Trout Lake, Riley Park, West End and Kitsilano farmers markets operate in spaces that are increasingly restricted and under-resourced. Markets are being displaced.

One of the actions in our 2022-26 strategic plan is “securing functional solutions for markets facing displacement by construction” (in 2023, we removed the word “construction”). Market spaces are subject to the same development, construction, resource and co-ordination pressures facing most of Vancouver’s social and economic infrastructure. But markets are not on the planning and development agenda — they’re special events. If Vancouver wants markets to continue to be part of its social, economic and climate-resilient landscape, the city will need to be intentional about making space for them before they’re squeezed out.

Call it a warning, but the opportunity is ripe!

Let’s talk about Glorious Organics. A Michelin-revered co-operative farm out of Aldergrove, Glorious Organics and Friesen Farm form the collective Organic Farm Connection, which has been a permanent fixture at the Trout Lake, Kitsilano and Riley Park markets for decades. Their certified organic produce is a staple at farmers markets and restaurants. Faced with growing piles of produce and increased customers crammed into their 20-by-27-foot stall space — particularly in the last five years — Mark Cormier and Ann Friesen have been applying for more space. But the markets don’t have any to give.

Cropthorne Farm has encountered this lack of space too, and for Lydia Ryall, who started her certified organic family farm on Westham Island in 2009, there’s a tension between making space for her tents, her truck and her customers. Year-round, the Cropthorne stall is one of the most popular, diverse and abundant at the West End, Kitsilano and Riley Park markets, making over 50 types of mixed certified organic vegetables available to Vancouver residents. Multiple days a week, the Cropthorne team displays piles of produce and manages a lineup of customers, but bringing all those vegetables to Vancouver neighbourhoods also means driving, unloading, moving and parking the truck — a labour and space trade-off that might not be necessary if Vancouver had more functional market space.

The need for market space is similar for urban food startups.

When Ben Healy — a 28-year-old Irish immigrant and a trained cook — joined Vancouver Farmers Markets in 2025, he brought something deeply personal to the market: traditional Irish brown bread inspired by the food culture of his home, customized with local grain available here in B.C. Today, Healy’s Irish Brown Bread sells across several Vancouver Farmers Markets locations, which have offered Healy a platform to build a business in his new home. What does he need to keep growing his business? He wants more dates.

For Natalie Cumberbirch of Merci Boulangerie, the market is another way of sharing a piece of home. Her French-inspired bakery, which joined Vancouver Farmers Markets in 2020, is her attempt to bring a little bit of Paris to Vancouver through croissants, pain au chocolat, baguettes and the experience of sharing good food with others. How does she afford the lease on her bricks-and-mortar bakery? Consistent market dates.

Trixie Ling founded the non-profit Flavours of Hope to help newcomer women entrepreneurs build and grow food businesses, using food, storytelling and entrepreneurship to bring people together across cultures. For newcomer entrepreneurs, markets provide something very fundamental: an accessible place to test an idea, meet customers and grow a business. When these women graduate the Dream Cuisines food business incubator program, what’s one of the biggest hurdles they face? Minimal access to market dates.

Every business and their food and story are different, and yet they share a common theme: they need viable, consistent spaces to run and grow a viable business.

“The greatest opportunity isn't simply improving permits or installing water, washrooms and electrification at temporary sites. It's creating a more co-ordinated municipal approach that aligns markets as low-cost, high-impact tools that support the city's existing goals around climate resilience, economic development, food systems, public space and healthy communities. Municipal leadership is required to champion the kind of change required to support farmers markets, communities and small businesses next year and into the future,” says Laura Smit, executive director of Vancouver Farmers Markets.

We’re telling more stories to demonstrate the need for municipalities to make space for markets on the ground, at the table and on the menu.

On the ground — consistent, accessible spaces designed to actually work for farmers, vendors, shoppers and the logistics of a market.
At the table — bringing market operators into planning conversations early on, before a public space has already been designed, or approved for new construction, and while there is still an opportunity to consult who gets impacted by a dislocated market.
On the menu — recognizing farmers markets as part of the city's long-term food system and community infrastructure, rather than treating them as temporary events that happen to occupy public space.

Does Vancouver need local food, thriving small businesses, vibrant public spaces and stronger community connections? We all know it does. The real question is whether we’re willing to build the conditions that allow the people already providing those things to continue doing so.

So, please don’t squeeze the tomatoes.

Give farmers ground to grow, give small businesses tables to build, and give communities menus to gather around and connect.

And, most importantly, make strategic space for farmers markets in Vancouver’s future.

There’s nothing like a celebration, and on Saturday, Sept. 19, the BC and Yukon Book Prizes celebrated the winners of the 42nd Book Prizes.

This year’s winners included Endling by Maria Reva, We Survived the Night by Julian Brave NoiseCat and Buzzkill Clamshell by Amber Dawn. A total of eight prizes were awarded along with the Lieutenant Governor’s Award for Literary Excellence and the Borealis Prize: The Commissioner of Yukon Award for Literary Contribution.

The award celebrations were punctuated by entertainment that combined unique poetry by local poets including 2017 Dorothy Livesay Poetry Prize winner Adèle Barclay, which was paired with drag performances by Tiffany Ann Co., AndrogynAss and Jaryd.

View photos and a full list of the 2026 winners here.
